guide.title: Unit 5: Poetry II: review guide
guide.intro: This unit compares poems built in fixed, closed forms with poems in open forms, and practices reading imagery, exaggeration, and the comparisons poets use to make one thing illuminate another.

sections.title: Closed and open forms
body: A closed form follows a set pattern of lines, rhyme, or meter. A sonnet, for example, has fourteen lines and a set rhyme scheme, and often turns in its final lines (in an English sonnet, a closing rhymed couplet). An open form, often called free verse, has no fixed rhyme or meter; its line breaks follow the movement of thought, breath, or emphasis.
Either way, ask what the form does: a rhyme can link two ideas, a closing couplet can sum up or overturn, and a short line in free verse can isolate a word or slow the reader down.
points: Describe the form, then explain its effect.
Look for a turn: a shift in tone, time, or idea, often marked by “but,” “now,” or a new stanza.

sections.title: Imagery and hyperbole
body: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses: sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Strong images make an experience concrete and often carry feeling, such as an empty branch suggesting loss.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration (“I have waited a thousand years”). It is not a lie; it signals intensity of feeling, often with humor.
points: Name the sense an image appeals to and the feeling it creates.
Tell the literal meaning (what is said) from the figurative meaning (what is suggested).

sections.title: Personification, allusion, and extended metaphor
body: Personification gives human traits to something nonhuman (doors that sigh, trees that keep secrets). An allusion is a brief reference to a well-known person, story, or event outside the poem; it brings that story's associations into the poem.

An extended metaphor develops one comparison across several lines or a whole poem, such as a kitchen described throughout as a ship. Track each part of the comparison and ask what the whole pattern suggests.
points: For an allusion, ask what the reference brings with it.
For an extended metaphor, map the parts: what stands for what?

example.prompt: A poem calls a grandmother's garden “her small republic, where every bean had a vote.” Identify the comparison and its effect.
example.solution: It is a metaphor (garden as republic) with personification (beans that vote). Together they suggest the garden is an orderly, fair world the grandmother governs, a playful way of showing her care and authority.

misconceptions: Free verse has no fixed pattern, but its line breaks and stanzas are still deliberate choices.
Hyperbole is obvious exaggeration used to show strong feeling or humor.
“An allusion is the same as a quotation.”
An allusion is a brief reference; it need not quote anything.
“A metaphor only lasts for one phrase.”
An extended metaphor can run through an entire poem.

passages.title: Poem 1: “Winter Orchard”
text: (1) The orchard keeps its counsel through the frost;
(2) each branch holds out a hand that nothing fills.
(3) The summer's sweetness, gathered up and lost,
(4) lies sleeping in the cellar on the sills.
(5) My father walked these rows when I was small
(6) and named each tree as if it were a friend;
(7) he swore he heard them whisper in the fall
(8) the secrets that a harvest has to end.
(9) Now I walk here alone, and I can hear
(10) no whisper but the wind along the wire,
(11) and yet I name them, Russet, Pippin, Pear,
(12) the way he did beside the kitchen fire.
(13) The trees forget us; we are what remains
(14) to tell their names, like prayers, to winter rains.

passages.title: Poem 2: “My Mother's Kitchen”
text: (1) My mother's kitchen is a ship
(2) that sails at six each morning,
(3) the stove its engine, humming,
(4) the table its long deck
(5) where we sit, a sleepy crew,
(6) waiting for orders.
(7) She stands at the wheel of the sink
(8) and steers us through the weather
(9) of homework, bills, a broken lunchbox,
(10) and when the storm of the school bus
(11) horn blows from the street,
(12) she lowers each of us
(13) like a lifeboat
(14) into the day.

passages.title: Poem 3: “Monday”
text: (1) I have waited for this bus a thousand years.
(2) Empires have risen and fallen at this stop;
(3) the pyramids were young when I arrived.
(4) Like Penelope, I have watched the road
(5) for one familiar shape, and found
(6) only the 7:40, late, and full,
(7) its doors sighing shut in my face.
(8) I will wait another thousand.
(9) I will grow a beard of moss.

passages.title: Poem 4: “Market at Dawn”
text: (1) Before the sun, the market wakes in crates:
(2) the hiss of ice poured over silver fish,
(3) the thud of melons, green and striped as drums,
(4) the bitter steam of coffee in a cup
(5) a vendor holds with both hands, like a nest.
(6) By seven, it is noise and haggling, coins,
(7) a child asleep on sacks of onions, gulls.
(8) By noon, the stalls fold up their canvas wings
(9) and the whole street flies off, and leaves behind
(10) a single crushed tomato on the stones.

questions.prompt: The form of the poem is best described as
choices: a prose poem written in paragraphs
a haiku sequence of three-line stanzas
free verse with no rhyme and no regular line length, which lets the speaker's memories flow freely
a closed form: fourteen lines with a regular rhyme scheme ending in a couplet
questions.explanation: The poem has fourteen lines, rhymes in alternating pairs (frost/lost, fills/sills), and ends with a rhymed couplet (remains/rains): a closed, sonnet-like form.
choiceExplanations: It is written in lines, not paragraphs.
It is not built from three-line stanzas.
The lines rhyme in a regular pattern.

questions.prompt: In lines 1–2, the orchard that “keeps its counsel” and the branch that “holds out a hand” are examples of
choices: allusion
hyperbole
personification
onomatopoeia, words that imitate sounds
questions.explanation: Keeping counsel (staying silent about secrets) and holding out a hand are human actions given to trees: personification.
choiceExplanations: No outside person, story, or event is referred to.
Nothing is exaggerated.
No word imitates a sound.

questions.prompt: The image of a branch holding out “a hand that nothing fills” (line 2) suggests
choices: emptiness and loss after the harvest
a threat of violence
the generosity of the orchard's owner
the abundance of the coming spring
questions.explanation: An open, empty hand evokes something missing; in winter the branches are bare, and the speaker's father is gone.
choiceExplanations: Nothing violent is suggested.
The image is of emptiness, not giving.
The poem looks back at a lost summer, not ahead to spring.

questions.prompt: The closing couplet (lines 13–14) functions mainly to
choices: turn from personal memory to a broader claim that people keep alive what nature forgets
repeat the opening line word for word to show that nothing has changed since the father's death
describe the next summer's harvest
introduce a new character who will continue the father's work
questions.explanation: After twelve lines of memory, the couplet generalizes (“The trees forget us; we are what remains”): the form's final rhyme marks a turn to a larger idea about memory.
choiceExplanations: The couplet does not repeat line 1.
The couplet speaks of winter rains, not a harvest.
No new character appears; “we” includes the speaker and people in general.

questions.prompt: Unlike a closed form such as a sonnet, this poem
choices: is a fourteen-line sonnet ending in a couplet
follows a strict rhyme scheme in every stanza
repeats a refrain at the end of each stanza
is in free verse, with line breaks that follow the thought
questions.explanation: The lines vary in length, do not rhyme, and break where the images break (“like a lifeboat / into the day”): an open form.
choiceExplanations: It has no couplet and no sonnet pattern.
The lines do not rhyme regularly.
No line is repeated as a refrain.

questions.prompt: The comparison that runs throughout the poem is best described as
choices: personification of the stove alone
an extended metaphor comparing the kitchen to a ship
a single simile used only in the first line and then dropped
an allusion to a famous voyage in history
questions.explanation: The kitchen is a ship; the stove its engine; the table its deck; the children its crew; the mother steers at the wheel. One comparison developed across the poem is an extended metaphor.
choiceExplanations: The stove is one part of a larger comparison.
The ship comparison continues for the whole poem.
No specific historical voyage is mentioned.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Lines 8–9, in which the mother “steers us through the weather / of homework, bills, a broken lunchbox,” present everyday problems as
choices: storms the mother navigates, giving ordinary troubles a voyage's drama
pleasant activities the family enjoys together
literal bad weather that keeps the children home from school and makes the morning difficult
problems the children cause on purpose
questions.explanation: The weather image turns homework and bills into rough seas, so the mother's daily coping becomes skilled navigation.
choiceExplanations: Bills and a broken lunchbox are troubles, not pleasures.
The weather is figurative; the problems are homework and bills.
Nothing suggests the children cause problems on purpose.

questions.prompt: In lines 12–14, the simile “like a lifeboat” adds to the extended metaphor by suggesting that the mother
choices: is unable to keep the family together
abandons her children because the ship is sinking and she must save herself first
sends her children out with care, though they must leave the ship
wishes she could leave the kitchen herself
questions.explanation: A lifeboat is lowered with care to carry people safely; the mother sends each child “into the day” with the same protective care.
choiceExplanations: She is shown in control throughout the poem.
The ship is not sinking; the “storm” is only the bus horn.
Nothing suggests she wants to leave.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

choices: rhyme, to link each line to the next
literal historical facts about empires
understatement, making the wait seem shorter than it was
hyperbole, exaggerating the wait for comic effect
questions.explanation: No one waits a thousand years or since the pyramids were young; the exaggeration humorously conveys the speaker's frustration.
choiceExplanations: The lines do not rhyme.
Empires and pyramids are exaggerations, not history lessons.
The lines inflate the wait rather than shrinking it.

questions.prompt: The reference to Penelope in line 4 is
choices: a personification of the road
an allusion to a mythic figure known for long waiting
an image appealing to the sense of smell
an extended metaphor that runs through the whole poem, comparing the speaker to a wife
questions.explanation: Penelope, in Homer's Odyssey, waited twenty years for Odysseus. The brief reference is an allusion that brings the idea of faithful, endless waiting into the poem.
choiceExplanations: The road is not given human traits here.
It is a reference to a story, not a sensory image.
The reference appears once; it is not developed through the poem.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: In line 7, the bus doors “sighing shut” are an example of
choices: an allusion to a famous bus
hyperbole about the length of the wait, like the exaggeration in lines 1–3
personification that makes the bus seem dismissive
a closed form
questions.explanation: Sighing is a human act; the doors seem weary or dismissive as they close in the speaker's face.
choiceExplanations: No outside story is referred to.
The phrase describes the doors, not the length of the wait.
Closed form refers to a poem's structure, not a phrase.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-08); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: The short, flat final lines (lines 8–9) mainly serve to
choices: continue the comic exaggeration while sounding resigned
resolve the conflict by having the bus finally arrive with room for the speaker
shift to serious grief over a lost love
introduce a regular rhyme scheme
questions.explanation: “I will wait another thousand” and the “beard of moss” keep the joke going, but the brief declarative lines sound tired and resigned.
choiceExplanations: The bus has come and gone full; nothing is resolved.
Penelope is a comic comparison; the poem stays wry, not grieving.
Lines 8–9 do not rhyme.

questions.prompt: Lines 2–4 present the market mainly through
choices: abstract statements about the economy of the market
sensory images of sound, sight, and smell
a single image of touch
a dialogue between vendors
questions.explanation: The hiss of ice and thud of melons (sound), silver fish and striped melons (sight), and bitter steam of coffee (smell) make the scene concrete.
choiceExplanations: The lines are concrete, not abstract.
Several senses are involved, not touch alone.
No one speaks.

questions.prompt: The poem is organized mainly by
choices: a contrast between the city and the countryside
a debate between two speakers
the passage of time from before sunrise to noon
a list of reasons for visiting a market
questions.explanation: The markers “Before the sun,” “By seven,” and “By noon” move the poem through the market's day.
choiceExplanations: The whole poem stays in the market street.
There is only one voice.
The poem describes, it does not argue.

questions.prompt: In lines 8–9, the stalls that “fold up their canvas wings” and the street that “flies off” develop
choices: an allusion to the myth of Icarus
a metaphor comparing the market to a flock of birds
hyperbole about the price of food
a personification of the child asleep on the onion sacks
questions.explanation: Wings and flying, echoing the gulls of line 7, turn the packing-up market into a flock taking off.
choiceExplanations: Nothing refers to Icarus or any myth.
Prices are not mentioned.
The child appears earlier and is not part of this image.

questions.prompt: The final image of “a single crushed tomato on the stones” (line 10) mainly serves to
choices: suggest that violence occurred in the market
symbolize the vendors' wealth
criticize the vendors for being careless and for leaving their waste behind on the street
show, through one leftover detail, how completely the market has vanished
questions.explanation: After the crowded lists of the earlier lines, a single crushed tomato is all that is left: the contrast stresses the emptiness after the market leaves.
choiceExplanations: The tomato is a leftover, not evidence of violence.
A crushed tomato suggests the opposite of wealth.
The tone is observant, not critical.
